report:
Your instinct is right for **typical knee osteoarthritis**: arthroscopic lavage/debridement generally does **not** help and is not recommended.

The key evidence is a sham-controlled NEJM trial: 180 patients with knee OA were randomized to arthroscopic debridement, lavage, or placebo surgery; outcomes after real arthroscopy were **no better than placebo** (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259). A later Cochrane review of arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease found little to no clinically important benefit versus placebo/non-surgical care, with potential harms (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease). Reflecting this, AAOS states: “Arthroscopy with lavage and/or debridement in patients with a primary diagnosis of knee osteoarthritis is not recommended” (https://www.aaos.org/globalassets/quality-and-practice-resources/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/oak3cpg.pdf).

Important nuance: “no” applies to pain/stiffness from OA itself. Guidelines carve out a narrow exception for a **clear history of true mechanical locking**—not merely giving way, crepitus, or X-ray loose bodies—where referral may be considered (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/documents/evidence-review-16). Otherwise, evidence supports exercise/physiotherapy, weight management, analgesia, and selected injections or replacement for advanced disease.
